strengths: Addresses a fundamental limitation of unsupervised SAEs in diffusion models—feature splitting—by introducing supervised concept-latent assignment, ensuring concepts are centralized into individual latents.
Significantly streamlines inference-time unlearning: steering a single latent per concept eliminates combinatorial searches over latent subsets, reducing the hyperparameter search space by over 96%.

Delivers strong empirical performance on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, outperforming existing fine-tuning and mechanistic unlearning baselines across Unlearning Accuracy (UA), In-domain Retain Accuracy (IRA), and Cross-domain Retain Accuracy (CRA).

Demonstrates robust behavior in challenging settings, including sequential multi-concept unlearning (up to 9 objects), adversarial prompt resilience under UnlearnDiffAtk, and NSFW removal on the I2P benchmark.

The paper is clearly structured and well-supported by extensive ablations and analyses, including comparisons of loss variants (e.g., global cross-entropy vs. concept assignment), correlation studies, and k-NN probe validations.
weaknesses: Supervised assignment introduces a scalability bottleneck: unlike standard unsupervised SAEs that discover semantic features post-hoc, SAEMNESIA requires knowing target concepts a priori and generating paired activation datasets. Removing newly requested or unseen concepts would require additional training or fine-tuning.

The core single-latent premise is challenged in open-domain / complex tasks such as nudity unlearning on I2P, where steering a single latent achieved poor suppression (47 detections) and required relaxing to two latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) with a very large multiplier (-60).

Experiments are restricted to older U-Net architectures (Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v1.5). Validation on modern diffusion transformers (e.g., DiT, SDXL, or Flux) would significantly strengthen the claim of architecture agnosticism.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in mechanistic interpretability for diffusion models: feature splitting in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which previously required expensive combinatorial searches over latent subsets to achieve concept unlearning.

The proposed supervised formulation (incorporating Concept Assignment and Decorrelation losses) successfully enforces feature centralization, enabling single-latent (or very low latent) concept steering and reducing inference-time hyperparameter search by ~96.7%.

Strong empirical results across multiple evaluation axes: outperforms existing fine-tuning and mechanistic baselines on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark (91.51% average metric), exhibits markedly better scalability in sequential unlearning (up to 9 objects), and shows improved robustness against adversarial attacks (UnlearnDiffAtk).

Extensive experimental validation and ablations in both main text and appendix, including k-NN feature centralization validation, score distribution comparisons, uniform multiplier sweeps, and patch-level activation visualizations.
weaknesses: Requires explicit concept supervision during SAE training: Unlike unsupervised SAEs or zero-shot text-encoder editing methods, the concept vocabulary must be known in advance to generate training activations. Adding a new concept to unlearn typically requires collecting new data and fine-tuning the SAE with new latent assignments.

Dependence on structured synthetic prompt templates: The training activations are collected from rigid templates ('An image of {object} in {style}'). It remains unclear whether the centralized latents retain equal specificity and disentanglement under complex, naturalistic, or compositional prompts containing multiple overlapping objects.

Discrepancy with the single-latent claim in complex real-world concepts: While the core narrative emphasizes single-neuron steering, the nudity removal experiment on I2P requires steering two latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) because single-latent steering yields suboptimal suppression (47 detections vs. 18 for SAeUron), highlighting limitations when concepts cannot be cleanly isolated into a single neuron.

Experiments are limited to older UNet-based architectures (SD v1.4 / v1.5): Although the methodology is described as architecture-agnostic, modern text-to-image foundation models predominantly employ Diffusion Transformers (DiTs, e.g., SD3, FLUX). Demonstrating applicability on at least one DiT-based model would significantly broaden the paper's impact.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Directly addresses feature splitting in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), which previously hindered mechanistic unlearning by scattering semantic concepts across multiple latents.

Substantial inference-time efficiency gains: By enforcing feature centralization through the proposed Concept Assignment and Decorrelation losses, the inference-time hyperparameter search is reduced by ~96.7% compared to SAeUron (evaluating only a scalar multiplier per concept rather than combinatorial latent subsets).

Solid empirical performance on standard benchmarks: SAEMNESIA achieves strong results on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark (91.51% average of UA, IRA, and CRA), outperforming existing fine-tuning and SAE-based baselines.

Comprehensive validation of representation properties: The authors provide thorough analyses, including k-NN probing across denoising timesteps showing that the single top latent retains concept discriminability comparable to the full feature set, score distribution histograms, and sequential unlearning up to 9 concepts.

Extensive appendix with ablations: Includes insightful investigations into loss variants (global cross-entropy vs. sigmoid CA loss, pre- vs. post-TopK), from-scratch vs. fine-tuned SAEs, and concept overlap (e.g., the challenging Dogs vs. Cats case).
weaknesses: Supervision bottleneck compromises the post-hoc nature of SAEs: Requiring supervised prompt-activation pairs and retraining/fine-tuning the SAE for specific concepts limits the fundamental advantage of unsupervised SAEs (i.e., general-purpose, open-ended post-hoc discovery and steering). Unlearning an unindexed concept requires gathering data and fine-tuning the SAE again.

Single-latent hypothesis breaks down on complex concepts: For nudity removal on the I2P benchmark (Appendix 6.11), the single-latent approach underperforms significantly (47 detections vs. SAeUron's 18), forcing the authors to resort to steering two latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) and a very aggressive multiplier (-60). This reveals that true one-to-one concept centralization struggles with broad, multi-faceted concepts.

Evaluation restricted to legacy models (SD v1.4 and v1.5): The empirical validation is entirely conducted on older UNet-based architectures. Modern text-to-image backbones (e.g., DiT-based models such as SD3, FLUX, or PixArt) are not tested, leaving open the question of whether this specific cross-attention block intervention and supervised SAE formulation transfer well to modern architectures.

Localization to a single UNet block: The method relies exclusively on extracting activations from block `up.1.1`. While empirically effective for the evaluated object classes, different concept granularities (e.g., compositions, actions, fine textures) may not localize cleanly to this single layer.

strengths: Clear motivation and effective conceptual framework: Directly addresses the known limitation of feature splitting in unsupervised Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) by introducing supervised concept-latent assignment and decorrelation constraints, achieving feature centralization.

Substantial operational efficiency gains: By localizing each concept to a single latent neuron (or a very small fixed set), the inference-time hyperparameter search space across latent combinations is eliminated, reducing search cost by ~96.7% compared to combinatorial searches in SAeUron.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements: Outperforms the state-of-the-art SAE-based unlearning baseline (SAeUron) across the board on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark (+9.22% average score on objects), exhibits better adversarial robustness under both white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) attacks, and maintains higher accuracy during sequential multi-concept unlearning.

Modular and reversible design: Because unlearning operates via inference-time activation steering of an attached SAE, the base diffusion model weights remain untouched, preserving full reversibility and modularity.

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analyses: The paper provides extensive validations of feature centralization via k-NN classification, score distribution histograms, cross-concept confusion matrices, and multiple architectural/loss variants in the appendix.
weaknesses: Supervision requirement: Unlike purely unsupervised dictionary learning approaches that discover latent directions without prompt-level supervision, SAEmnesia relies on labeled concept prompts and pre-specified anchor prompts, making it less readily extensible to arbitrary out-of-vocabulary concepts without additional fine-tuning or score computation.

Evaluation largely confined to U-Net Stable Diffusion v1.4/v1.5: The primary experiments focus on older architectures; while SD v1.5 is standard for UnlearnCanvas, validation on modern rectified-flow and transformer-based diffusion models (e.g., FLUX, SD3) is absent beyond preliminary and inconclusive SDXL-Turbo results.

Limitations on complex concepts and intra-class entanglement: For concepts such as nudity (I2P), a single latent proved insufficient (yielding 47 detections), requiring post-hoc expansion to two latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) to achieve competitive performance. Moreover, the decorrelation loss is only applied across macro-groups (e.g., objects vs. styles), leaving fine-grained intra-group entanglement (e.g., Cats vs. Dogs) partially unaddressed.

strengths: Clear motivation and conceptually sound formulation: Addressing feature splitting in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) by enforcing one-to-one concept-neuron mappings via supervised concept assignment and inter-group decorrelation is intuitive and effective.

Significant practical and computational improvements over unsupervised SAE baselines: Eliminating combinatorial latent searches reduces inference hyperparameter tuning by over 96%, while single-latent steering achieves higher unlearning accuracy (+9.22% on UnlearnCanvas objects) and better retention than SAeUron.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors validate the method across multiple critical axes, including sequential multi-concept erasure, white-box (UnlearnDiffAtk) and black-box (Ring-A-Bell) adversarial robustness, k-NN representational localization, and NSFW erasure on the I2P benchmark.

Extensive ablation studies and transparency: The appendix thoroughly evaluates various architectural design choices (from-scratch vs. fine-tuned, global cross-entropy vs. concept assignment, pre- vs. post-TopK supervision) and provides detailed per-concept confusion heatmaps.
weaknesses: Generalization to held-out / open-vocabulary concepts is limited: Because concept centralization relies on explicit supervision during training, unlearning performance drops significantly on unseen held-out concepts (e.g., UA drops to ~53% on held-out styles in Table 17), diminishing the practical advantage of the supervised mapping in open-vocabulary settings.

Within-group concept entanglement remains an issue: As acknowledged by the authors and illustrated in the confusion matrices (Figures 13 and 14), decorrelation is only enforced across macro-categories (objects vs. styles) rather than within categories, leading to notable cross-concept interference between related visual classes (e.g., Dogs vs. Cats, Humans vs. other classes).

Inconsistency in single-latent sufficiency for complex concepts: On the I2P nudity erasure task (Table 13), steering a single latent underperforms the baseline (47 detections vs. 18 detections for SAeUron), requiring ad-hoc manual expansion to two latents (SAEMNESIA-TOP2) to achieve superior suppression, which somewhat compromises the single-latent erasure claim.

Evaluation is predominantly confined to older U-Net architectures: Experiments are almost entirely conducted on Stable Diffusion v1.4/v1.5. The preliminary exploration on SDXL-Turbo in Appendix A.13 shows a substantial drop in retention accuracy (IRA drops to 45.15%), and modern diffusion transformers (e.g., DiT, Flux) are not evaluated.

strengths: Addresses a concrete and important bottleneck in SAE-based concept erasure: feature splitting often spreads semantic concepts across multiple latents in unsupervised SAEs, creating an expensive combinatorial search space during unlearning.

Significant inference-time search efficiency: enforcing one-to-one concept-to-latent mapping reduces the steering hyperparameter search space from 210 configurations down to 7 (a 96.67% reduction) by removing the need to search over combinations of top latents.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper tests unlearning performance on UnlearnCanvas (both object and style), sequential concept unlearning, adversarial evaluations (white-box UnlearnDiffAtk and black-box Ring-A-Bell), and I2P nudity removal.

Non-destructive and fully reversible editing: because editing occurs via the external SAE rather than fine-tuning or pruning diffusion model weights, the base model remains entirely untouched and can be restored instantly.
Extensive ablations provided in the appendix, including scratch vs. fine-tuned variants, loss component breakdowns (CA, DC, CE), and sensitivity analysis across multiplier ranges.
weaknesses: Supervision diminishes unsupervised mechanistic discovery: standard SAEs are valued for unsupervised dictionary learning that surfaces latent structures organically. Requiring curated anchor prompts and predefined concept labels restricts the framework to a supervised/closed-vocabulary paradigm.

Limited generalization to unseen/held-out concepts: while the authors evaluate held-out style erasure in Appendix A.15 (Table 17), the unlearning accuracy drops substantially to 53.07% (from ~96% on seen styles), indicating that feature centralization does not readily transfer to unseen concepts without retraining.

Formulation of Concept Assignment Loss: Equation (8) penalizes assigned latents when target concepts are present, but lacks an explicit negative penalty when target concepts are absent (relying solely on L1 regularization). This can allow latents to activate spuriously on unrelated inputs, contributing to within-group concept interference (e.g., cats vs. dogs overlap).

Struggles on modern backbones: the preliminary SDXL-Turbo evaluation in Appendix A.13 shows an In-domain Retain Accuracy (IRA) drop to 45.15%, suggesting the method currently faces severe transferability challenges to newer diffusion and rectified flow architectures (e.g., SDXL, Flux).
